exercises.front: What are "accruals" (accrued expenses) in a balance sheet, and what is their French equivalent?
exercises.back: Accruals are expenses that have been incurred during the period but not yet invoiced or paid at the reporting date (e.g. electricity consumed in December but invoiced after year-end). They are recognised as a liability under the accrual basis of accounting. French equivalent: "charges à payer" (e.g. PCG account 408 "Fournisseurs – factures non parvenues"). Do not confuse with "prepayments" (charges constatées d'avance) or "deferred income" (produits constatés d'avance).
exercises.explanation: Under the accrual basis, the effects of transactions are recognised when they occur, not when cash is paid or received. An expense incurred in the period but not yet invoiced is therefore recorded as an expense against a liability (accrual). The mirror items are prepayments (an expense paid in advance, carried as an asset) and deferred income (revenue received in advance, carried as a liability).
exercises.source_ref: IAS 8 §6M-6N, accrual basis of accounting (formerly IAS 1 §27-28) — règlement UE 2023/1803 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/338 ; PCG compte 408

exercises.statement:
Extract from the statement of financial position of Harbour Tools Ltd at 31 December 2025 (€k): property, plant and equipment 900; inventories 180; trade receivables 240; cash and cash equivalents 60; share capital and reserves 620; long-term borrowings 400; trade payables 250; short-term borrowings 70; accruals 40.

Calculate the company's current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities). Round to two decimal places.
exercises.explanation: Current assets = inventories 180 + trade receivables 240 + cash and cash equivalents 60 = €480k. Current liabilities = trade payables 250 + short-term borrowings 70 + accruals 40 = €360k. Current ratio = 480 ÷ 360 = 1.33. Property, plant and equipment (non-current asset) and long-term borrowings (non-current liability) are excluded. Classic errors: excluding inventories gives the quick ratio (300 ÷ 360 = 0.83); adding the long-term borrowings to the denominator gives 480 ÷ 760 = 0.63.
exercises.source_ref: IFRS 18 §96-102, classification of current and non-current assets and liabilities (formerly IAS 1 §66-76) — règlement UE 2023/1803 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/338

exercises.statement:
Clearwater Foods plc presents its income statement by function. Extract for 2025 (€k): revenue 5,200; cost of sales 3,100 (including depreciation of production equipment: 260); distribution costs 600; administrative expenses 700 (including amortisation of software: 40); other operating income 50; finance costs 120; income tax expense 180. There are no other depreciation, amortisation or impairment charges.

Calculate EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation), in €k.
exercises.explanation: Operating profit = revenue 5,200 − cost of sales 3,100 − distribution costs 600 − administrative expenses 700 + other operating income 50 = €850k. Depreciation and amortisation are embedded in the functional expense lines, so they must be added back: EBITDA = 850 + 260 (depreciation) + 40 (amortisation) = €1,150k. Finance costs and income tax are below operating profit and are not deducted. Classic errors: stopping at operating profit (850); starting from profit before tax (850 − 120 = 730, then 730 + 300 = 1,030); confusing EBITDA with gross profit (5,200 − 3,100 = 2,100).
exercises.source_ref: IFRS 18 §78-83 (analysis of operating expenses by function; formerly IAS 1 §99-105) and §118(b) (operating profit before depreciation, amortisation and IAS 36 impairments is not a management-defined performance measure) — règlement UE 2023/1803 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/338 ; IAS 16 §6 and IAS 38 §8 (depreciation, amortisation) — règlement UE 2023/1803

exercises.statement: In a statement of cash flows prepared under IAS 7, which of the following cash flows is classified as an investing activity (flux d'investissement)?
options: Cash received from customers for goods held for resale
Proceeds from the disposal of a warehouse
Dividends paid to the company's shareholders
Cash paid for the principal portion of lease liabilities
exercises.explanation: Option 2 is correct: cash receipts from sales of property, plant and equipment are investing cash flows (IAS 7 §16(b)). Option 1 is wrong: cash receipts from the sale of goods are the typical operating cash flow (IAS 7 §14(a)). Option 3 is wrong: dividends paid are classified within financing activities (IAS 7 §33A, as amended by IFRS 18 for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027; before that date, financing or operating activities under former §34), never within investing activities. Option 4 is wrong: cash payments for the principal portion of lease liabilities are classified within financing activities (IFRS 16 §50(a), IAS 7 §17).
exercises.source_ref: IAS 7 §14, §16, §17 and §33A (as amended by IFRS 18, Regulation (EU) 2026/338) ; IFRS 16 §50 (règlement UE 2023/1803)

exercises.statement: Mayfield plc prepares its statement of cash flows for the financial year 2026 under IAS 7 (IFRS 18 does not yet apply). Which of the following presentations is NOT permitted?
options: Payments for short-term leases (12 months or less) for which the recognition exemption is applied, presented within operating activities
Interest paid presented within financing activities
Dividends paid to the shareholders of Mayfield presented within investing activities
Repayments of the principal portion of lease liabilities presented within financing activities
exercises.explanation: Option 3 is not permitted: dividends paid may be classified as financing (a cost of obtaining financial resources) or as operating activities (to show the ability to pay dividends out of operating cash flows), but never as investing activities (IAS 7 §34). The other presentations are permitted or required. Option 1: payments for short-term leases and leases of low-value assets not recognised on the balance sheet (exemption of IFRS 16 §5-6) are classified within operating activities (IFRS 16 §50(c)). Option 2: interest paid may be classified as operating or financing activities, consistently from period to period (IAS 7 §31 and §33). Option 4: cash payments for the principal portion of a lease liability are financing activities (IFRS 16 §50(a)).

exercises.title: Reading the accounts of Ashby Components Ltd
exercises.context:
You work for the French parent company of Ashby Components Ltd, a UK subsidiary. Its finance director has sent you an extract of the statement of financial position at 31 December 2025 (£k), prepared under IFRS.

Non-current assets: property, plant and equipment 1,250 ; intangible assets 180.
Current assets: inventories 320 ; trade receivables 410 ; prepayments 30 ; cash and cash equivalents 140.
Equity: share capital 400 ; retained earnings 850.
Liabilities: trade payables 380 ; accruals 60 ; current tax payable 40 ; bank loan 600, of which 100 is repayable in 2026 and 500 in 2029.

The finance director adds: "During the year we paid a dividend of £150k to the parent company and did not issue any new shares."

sub_questions.prompt: Calculate the quick ratio (current assets − inventories) ÷ current liabilities at 31 December 2025. Round to two decimal places.
sub_questions.explanation: Current assets = 320 + 410 + 30 + 140 = 900. Current liabilities = 380 + 60 + 40 + 100 (portion of the loan repayable within twelve months) = 580. Quick ratio = (900 − 320) ÷ 580 = 580 ÷ 580 = 1.00. Forgetting the current portion of the loan gives 580 ÷ 480 = 1.21; treating the whole loan as current gives 580 ÷ 1,080 = 0.54.

sub_questions.prompt: The £500k of the bank loan repayable in 2029 is presented as a current liability.
sub_questions.explanation: It is due more than twelve months after the reporting period: it is a non-current liability (IAS 1 §69, now IFRS 18 §101). Only the £100k repayable in 2026 is current.

sub_questions.prompt: In which primary statement will the £150k dividend appear as a movement in retained earnings?
sub_questions.explanation: Dividends are distributions to owners: the statement of changes in equity must reconcile each component of equity, showing separately the distributions to owners (IAS 1 §106(d)(iii), now IFRS 18 §107(c)(iii)), so the £150k reduction of retained earnings appears there, not as an expense in profit or loss or in OCI. "Notes only" is wrong: IAS 1 §107 (now IFRS 18 §110) lets the entity give the amount of dividends and the dividend per share either in that statement or in the notes, but the movement itself must appear in the statement of changes in equity. The dividend also appears as a cash outflow in the statement of cash flows (financing or operating activities in 2025; financing activities only from 2027, IAS 7 §33A as amended by IFRS 18).

sub_questions.prompt: For your French colleagues, give the French equivalent of: trade receivables, prepayments, accruals, retained earnings, cash and cash equivalents, current tax payable.
sub_questions.model_answer: Trade receivables: créances clients. Prepayments: charges constatées d'avance. Accruals: charges à payer. Retained earnings: réserves et report à nouveau (résultats accumulés). Cash and cash equivalents: trésorerie et équivalents de trésorerie. Current tax payable: dette d'impôt exigible (impôt sur les bénéfices à payer).
key_points: Trade receivables = créances clients ; prepayments = charges constatées d'avance
Accruals = charges à payer (passif), not « produits à recevoir »
Retained earnings = réserves et report à nouveau
Cash and cash equivalents = trésorerie et équivalents de trésorerie ; current tax payable = dette d'impôt exigible

exercises.explanation: The case tests the current / non-current split (IAS 1 §66-76, now IFRS 18 §96-102), the quick ratio, the statement in which distributions to owners are presented and the French equivalents of usual balance sheet items.
exercises.source_ref: IAS 1 §10, §66-76, §106(d) and §107, applicable to the 2025 accounts (règlement UE 2023/1803) ; now IFRS 18 §10, §96-102, §107 and §110 (règlement UE 2023/1803 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/338, financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027) ; quick ratio (usual definition)
